notes:
I couldn't search every site, so some parts of your list have gaps. I didn't read any NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Orthodox (oca.org), Lutheran, Pentecostal-specific or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace sources, so those are left out. Wesley's Notes are linked on Bible Hub, but I didn't open them. The one Methodist voice below is Adam Clarke, and only as David Guzik quotes him.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1 (the date)**
- Guzik says the dating is hard to follow. Some (like Morgan) believed this prophecy was delivered during the reign of Zedekiah but recalled events from the days of Jehoiakim. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) say the Holy Spirit has arranged Jeremiah's prophecies by the moral rather than the chronological connection. In their view the story was meant to teach the Jews who had just taken back their freed slaves (ch. 34). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_035.cfm
- Barnes places it between the battle of Carchemish and Nebuchadnezzar's arrival at Jerusalem, 17 years earlier than the narrative in Jeremiah 34:8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary dates it perhaps to the summer of B.C. 606. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-35.html

**v. 2 (who the Rechabites were; why the temple)**
- Most commentators trace them to the Kenites, the family of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law (1 Chr 2:55; Judg 1:16). Their founder Jonadab was the man who joined Jehu's purge of Ahab's house (2 Kgs 10). Guzik and JFB both say this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_035.cfm
- Barnes suggests Jonadab had two aims: keeping the purer morals of desert life, and protecting the tribe's freedom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm
- Why the temple? JFB says there were witnesses there, and Jeremiah could speak straight to the crowd. Citing Calvin, they add it may have rebuked priests who drank freely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm
- Benson argues that being let into the temple shows the Rechabites were not idolaters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm
- Ellicott says "house" means family. He sees Jonadab's way of life as a protest against Baal worship, city corruption and drunkenness, much like Elijah's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm

**v. 3 (the people named)**
- Ellicott notes that all three names contain God's name ("Jehovah hears / exalts / gathers"). He takes this as showing that the Rechabites were sharers in the faith of Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-3.htm
- Gill thinks the women may not have been brought along. Another note on the page calls Jaazaniah probably the then chief of the Rechabites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-3.htm

**v. 4 (the room)**
- Benson says the side rooms were used by priests and Levites and for storing sacred items. The "officials" were probably the leaders who met in council. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm
- Matthew Henry says Jeremiah chose a prophet's room, not the officials' room, because he was bringing a message from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-35.html
- Guzik, quoting Harrison, suggests "sons" may mean Hanan's disciples. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- Coffman reasons that if the whole clan fit in one room, it was probably not very large. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-35.html

**v. 5 ("Drink some wine")**
- Guzik points out that Jeremiah invited them but never commanded them in the Lord's name. The test was meant to show their faithfulness in public, not to make them give in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- The Restoration Commentary agrees: This is no example of placing a temptation before a weaker brother. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-35.html

**vv. 6–7 (Jonadab's rules)**
- Constable: Abstinence was not a requirement of the Mosaic Law; it was simply a requirement that Jonadab imposed on his family. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-35.html
- The Restoration Commentary links the ban on farming to Baal, an agricultural deity, the god of the farmer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-35.html
- Matthew Henry reads it practically: strangers in the land who "keep low" will not stir up jealousy. Living in tents also taught them not to settle down in this world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-35.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm

**vv. 8–10 (they obeyed)**
- Coffman stresses that every member obeyed, at all times, in every detail. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-35.html
- The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary links their obedience to Proverbs and to Ephesians 6:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-35.html

**v. 11 (moving into Jerusalem)**
- JFB: Necessity sets aside all other laws. This is the Rechabites' excuse for their seeming disobedience to Jonadab in temporarily settling in a city. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_035.cfm
- Matthew Henry goes further: they would have tempted God, and not trusted him if they had not taken sensible steps to stay safe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/jeremiah-35.html
- The Pulpit Commentary sees a weakness here: people who live apart still need the city in a crisis. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-35.html

**vv. 12–16 (the lesson for Judah)**
- Matthew Henry sets out the contrasts. The Rechabites obeyed a mere man; the Jews disobeyed the eternal God. Jonadab gave his order once; God kept sending prophets. Jonadab left his family no estate; God had given Judah a land. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_035.cfm ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-35.html
- Guzik: God only asks from us what we are willing to give to other people or other things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- Bible.org notes that the verb "hear" comes up again and again in this chapter. The Rechabites "hear" but Judah does not! https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-35
- Calvin (on v. 15) says God asked nothing beyond what nature itself teaches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/35-15.html
- Constable: Jeremiah may have expected God to rebuke the Rechabites' odd lifestyle, but the Rechabites' chosen lifestyle was no problem to Yahweh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-35.html

**v. 17 (the judgment)**
- Guzik: the contrast with the Rechabites was further evidence of Judah's guilt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- JFB link the verse to Proverbs 1:24 and Isaiah 65:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm

**v. 18 (praise for the Rechabites)**
- Ellicott says the verse decides nothing about whether others must follow the rule. What God praised was their loyalty to a human rule that broke no divine law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch think this word was spoken at the end of the meeting. It is placed here to sharpen the warning to Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm

**v. 19 ("a man to stand before Me")**
- Guzik, quoting Cundall, calls "stand before" a technical phrase for privileged service, used of prophets, priests and kings. He also cites the Mishnah: Jonadab's descendants had a set day each year for bringing wood to the temple altar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- Keil and Delitzsch: the phrase means both the family's survival and its continued service of God, though not priestly service. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm
- JFB give two options: representatives who worship God, or simply that the family keeps existing. They say the Rechabites came back from exile. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_035.cfm
- Did they become Levites? Plumptre argued they were taken into the tribe of Levi (cited by Coffman). The Pulpit Commentary calls that "rash" and reads it as a mark of special favour. It also says "forever" has a limited sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-35.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-35.html

## Where Protestant teachers differ

**vv. 6–8, 18: does this passage teach total abstinence from alcohol?**
- Yes, or close to it: the Restoration Commentary prays that believers' lives will protest against the debauchery and drunkenness of this world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-35.html
- The Biblical Illustrator includes a sermon saying, we shall do well to say with the Rechabites, whoever may ask us to drink, "We will drink no wine." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/35-10.html
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the Rechabites the prototypes of the modern teetotalers. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-35.html
- No: another Biblical Illustrator sermon says abstinence from wine is not here made obligatory. It also asks whether a Rechabite could refuse the wine at Communion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/jeremiah-35.html
- Ellicott also says no, citing Matthew 11:19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm
- Guzik takes a middle line. The point is obedience, not wine, but God still honoured their abstinence and did not mock it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/

**v. 18: does this support binding human traditions and religious rules?**
- Reformed: JFB, citing Calvin, say what is praised here is not the father's injunction, but the obedience of the sons. They add that it gives no support to slavish respect for the church fathers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_035.cfm
- Calvin argues that rules setting up man-made worship are wicked. He says the "Papists" twist this passage to support their own laws. https://ccel.org/study/Jer_35
- Anglican: Ellicott, by contrast, praises faithfulness to a rule of life whether it be that of a school, a college, a guild, or a religious order. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/35-18.htm

**v. 19: was the Rechabites' obedience saving or not?**
- A Gospel Coalition writer is struck that God promises grace for obedience to a set of commands that have nothing to do with the covenant of God. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/rechabites-muslim-neighbour-reflections-jeremiah-35/
- A Biblical Illustrator sermon says Rechabite obedience was not necessary to salvation; Christian obedience is indispensable. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/jeremiah-35.html
- The Methodist Adam Clarke (quoted by Guzik) sees true Christians as their real successors. He also notes some think the Essenes descended from them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/

## Other views

**vv. 2, 6 (modern scholarship)**
- Guzik, quoting Cundall, says they were most likely a voluntary sect rather than the literal descendants of Jonadab. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-35/
- Ellicott suggests "son of Rechab" may mean "son of the chariot," that is, a disciple of Elijah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-2.htm
- Ellicott also suggests that "brothers" and "sons" in v. 3 may be grades of membership in a religious order. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-3.htm

**v. 18 (the text itself)**
- The Cambridge Bible says the Greek Old Testament (LXX), doubtless rightly, omit these words. The Hebrew then had to switch from "they" to "you." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests vv. 18–19 were perhaps removed from its original connection. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-35.html

**vv. 6–7 (Catholic)**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia says it was evidently the belief of Jonadab and the Rechabites that settled life with its forms of civilization led to apostasy. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12676a.htm
- Its "Asceticism" article says it is uncertain whether their abstinence was meant as penance. It may simply have been to keep them nomadic. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01767c.htm
- Its "Nazarite" article doubts that they took a Nazirite vow. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10727a.htm

**v. 19 (later history)**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that 19th-century temperance societies took the name "Rechabites." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14482a.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch report the missionary Joseph Wolff's claim of finding Rechabites in Yemen and Mesopotamia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/35-18.htm
